Amazon CloudWatch introduced metrics, logs, alarms and dashboards so AWS resource and application health could be operated from evidence rather than intuition.

Architecture / mental model

AWS resources/apps → metrics/logs/traces → CloudWatch → dashboards / queries / alarms → operator or automation

How it works

CloudWatch receives metrics from many AWS services and can ingest custom application metrics. Metrics are time-series measurements; logs preserve event text/fields; alarms evaluate metric conditions and can trigger notifications or automation.

A dashboard is useful only when its widgets answer operational questions. CPU alone rarely explains application health; latency, error rate, saturation, queue depth and dependency signals may matter more depending on the system.

CloudWatch Logs centralizes log streams and supports filtering/querying. The CloudWatch agent can collect additional host metrics and logs from EC2 when the built-in service metrics are not enough.

Hands-on reference

aws cloudwatch list-metrics --namespace AWS/EC2
aws cloudwatch describe-alarms
aws logs describe-log-groups

Verification

Pick one known event, such as CPU/load or an application error, and trace it from source to metric/log to dashboard/alarm. Then test the alarm condition in a safe lab instead of assuming notification wiring works.

Field note / gotcha

Monitoring data is not automatically meaningful because it exists. An alarm on the wrong metric or threshold can be perfectly functional and operationally useless.

Security considerations

Restrict log access, avoid writing secrets into logs and protect alarm/notification configuration from unauthorized changes that could blind operators.

What I learned

Observability begins when telemetry answers a decision, not when a dashboard contains many graphs.
